questions.title: WFA-M1 · Fundamental qualitative characteristics
questions.promptMarkdown: Under the IASB Conceptual Framework, which pair represents the two **fundamental** qualitative characteristics of useful financial information?
hints: Distinguish fundamental qualities from the four enhancing qualities.
Information must both matter to decisions and accurately depict economic substance.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: **Relevance** and **faithful representation** are the two fundamental qualitative characteristics; comparability, verifiability, timeliness, and understandability are *enhancing* characteristics.
questions.pitfall: Confusing enhancing characteristics (comparability/verifiability) with fundamental characteristics.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M2 · Asset recognition criteria on the SFP
questions.promptMarkdown: Nordic Design AS spends £40,000 training its sales staff on a new CRM system. How should this £40,000 expenditure be treated in the financial statements?
options: Capitalised as an intangible non-current asset and amortised over 5 years
Recognised immediately as an expense in the income statement because the firm lacks legal control over staff remaining
Recorded directly as a deduction from share capital without passing through profit
Held in current assets as prepaid employee goodwill
hints: Check the control test for an asset in Chapter 2.
Employees can resign, so future economic benefits from general training are not controlled by the entity.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Because the business cannot **control** employees' future service, staff training fails the asset recognition test and is expensed immediately in the income statement.
questions.pitfall: Capitalising internally incurred staff training or marketing spend as an intangible asset.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M3 · Double-entry effect of credit purchase settlement
questions.promptMarkdown: When a business pays £12,000 from its bank account to settle an existing trade payable (with no settlement discount), what is the double-entry effect?
options: Debit Trade payables £12,000; Credit Cash at bank £12,000 (equity unchanged)
Debit Cash at bank £12,000; Credit Trade payables £12,000 (equity unchanged)
Debit Purchases expense £12,000; Credit Cash at bank £12,000 (equity decreases)
Debit Trade payables £12,000; Credit Retained earnings £12,000 (equity increases)
hints: Decreasing a liability is a Debit; decreasing an asset is a Credit.
Was any revenue earned or new expense incurred at the moment of cash settlement?
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Paying a supplier reduces the liability **Trade payables** (**Debit £12,000**) and reduces the asset **Cash at bank** (**Credit £12,000**). Total assets and total liabilities fall equally; profit and equity are unaffected.
questions.pitfall: Treating supplier cash payment as an expense at settlement rather than when goods/services were incurred.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M4 · Accrued expense adjustment error
questions.promptMarkdown: If an accountant forgets to record £8,500 of accrued electricity expense at year-end, what is the effect on the year-end financial statements?
options: Profit is understated by £8,500 and current liabilities are overstated by £8,500
Profit is overstated by £8,500 and current liabilities are understated by £8,500
Profit is overstated by £8,500 and cash is overstated by £8,500
Assets are overstated by £8,500 and liabilities are unaffected
hints: Write the missing entry: Dr Electricity expense £8,500, Cr Accruals (current liability) £8,500.
Omitting an expense makes profit too high; omitting the accrual makes liabilities too low.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Omitting an accrued expense leaves expenses £8,500 too low (**profit & equity overstated by £8,500**) and omits the current liability (**current liabilities understated by £8,500**). Cash is unaffected.
questions.pitfall: Assuming accrued expenses affect the year-end cash balance.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M5 · Working capital impact on operating cash flow
questions.promptMarkdown: During 2026, operating profit is £90,000, depreciation is £18,000, inventories increased by £11,000, and trade payables increased by £7,000 (no other working capital items). Cash generated from operations is:
hints: Add back non-cash depreciation to operating profit.
An inventory build-up absorbs cash (−£11,000), whereas higher trade payables conserve cash (+£7,000).
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.pitfall: Flipping the signs on working capital changes (adding inventory increase or subtracting payable increase).

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M6 · Relevant cost of inventory already in stock
questions.promptMarkdown: A firm holds 400 kg of Specialty Alloy bought last year for £15/kg (historic cost £6,000). If not used on a one-off contract, it would be sold immediately as scrap for £9/kg; the alloy has no other use in the business. What is the relevant cost of using the 400 kg on the contract?
options: £0, because the alloy is already paid for
hints: Sunk purchase cost (£15/kg) is always irrelevant.
Ask what cash inflow the firm sacrifices by using the material instead of scrapping it.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: The historic £6,000 is sunk. Using the alloy sacrifices £9/kg in immediate scrap proceeds, so the relevant opportunity cost is $400 \times £9 = \mathbf{£3,600}$.
questions.pitfall: Treating existing material as free (£0) and ignoring its forgone scrap proceeds.

questions.title: WFA-M7 · Operating gearing and profit sensitivity
questions.promptMarkdown: Company H has high fixed costs and low variable cost per unit; Company L has low fixed costs and high variable cost per unit. At the same current sales volume and operating profit, if sales volume rises by 15%:
options: Company L's operating profit will increase by a larger percentage than Company H's
Company H's operating profit will increase by a larger percentage because its contribution margin ratio is higher
Both companies will experience the exact same 15% increase in operating profit
Company H has a lower break-even point when demand falls
hints: Recall operating gearing = Contribution / Operating profit.
High fixed costs with equal profit imply a larger total contribution, magnifying volume swings.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Company H has higher **operating gearing**: each extra unit sold generates a higher contribution while fixed costs stay constant, so profit rises (and falls) by a larger percentage than at Company L.
questions.pitfall: Mixing up operating gearing risk on the downside with profit sensitivity on the upside.

questions.title: WFA-M8 · Traditional volume-based costing vs ABC cross-subsidisation
questions.promptMarkdown: When a multi-product factory switches from a single direct-labour-hour (DLH) overhead rate to Activity-Based Costing (ABC), low-volume complex batch products typically show:
options: A lower unit cost under ABC because they consume fewer total labour hours
A higher unit cost under ABC because batch-level set-up and inspection costs are spread over fewer units
Unchanged unit cost, because total factory overhead is identical
Zero indirect cost, because ABC only traces direct materials
hints: Traditional DLH allocates set-up/inspection pools in proportion to volume.
Small complex batches trigger disproportionate set-ups per unit produced.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: Traditional volume-based rates **under-cost** low-volume complex products and **over-cost** high-volume standard products; ABC assigns batch-level set-ups/inspections accurately, raising the reported unit cost of small complex batches.
questions.pitfall: Assuming fewer total DLHs means complex small batches become cheaper under ABC.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M9 · Mutually exclusive projects: NPV vs IRR
questions.promptMarkdown: Projects X (initial outlay £50,000, IRR 22%, NPV +£14,000) and Y (initial outlay £200,000, IRR 17%, NPV +£29,000) are mutually exclusive at a 10% cost of capital with no capital rationing. To maximise shareholder wealth, the firm should:
options: Accept Project X because 22% IRR exceeds 17% IRR
Accept Project Y because it generates the higher positive Net Present Value (+£29,000)
Accept both X and Y because both have positive NPVs
Reject both until their IRRs are equal
hints: IRR is a percentage rate and ignores project scale.
Which metric directly measures absolute shareholder wealth added in today's pounds?
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: **NPV** directly measures absolute wealth creation in present-value monetary terms (+£29,000 vs +£14,000). For mutually exclusive projects, IRR suffers from the **scale problem**.
questions.pitfall: Ranking mutually exclusive projects of different sizes by IRR percentage instead of NPV.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-M10 · Working capital in NPV cash-flow schedules
questions.promptMarkdown: A 4-year project requires £25,000 of net working capital at $t = 0$, maintained throughout Years 1–4 and fully recovered at the end of Year 4 ($t = 4$) at a 10% discount rate. What is the net effect of working capital on the project's **NPV**?
options: £0, because −£25,000 at t=0 and +£25,000 at t=4 cancel out
Negative (−£7,924.66), because the t=4 recovery is discounted while the t=0 outflow is not
Negative (−£25,000), because working capital release is an accounting entry rather than cash
Positive (+£17,075.34), because working capital recovery adds to Year 4 profit
hints: Time value of money means tying up cash for 4 years carries an opportunity cost.
rubricChecks: Identified the governing accounting principle or formula
Eliminated common WISEflow distractor traps accurately
questions.solutionMarkdown: In undiscounted terms $-25,000 + 25,000 = 0$, but in present value $-25,000 + 25,000 / 1.10^4 = -25,000 + 17,075.34 = \mathbf{-£7,924.66}$. Tying up working capital reduces NPV by the lost time value.
questions.pitfall: Omitting the t=4 working capital release OR claiming t=0 and t=4 cancel in PV terms.

pacing.rationale: 4-point WISEflow MCQ (~3–4 min exam budget under 1 pt = 1 min rule).

questions.title: WFA-E1 · Nordic Craft Ltd · FIFO, Accruals, Income Statement & Equity (45 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Nordic Craft Ltd** has extracted the following information for the financial year ended **31 December 2026** (all currency figures in GBP):

| Item | Amount |
| --- | ---: |
| Credit sales revenue | 420,000 |
| Irrecoverable trade receivables written off during 2026 | 4,000 |
| Cash wages paid during 2026 | 140,000 |
| Unpaid December wages accrued at 31 Dec 2026 | 6,000 |
| Cash rent paid during 2026 (includes 8,000 prepaid for Jan–Feb 2027) | 48,000 |
| Other cash operating expenses | 55,000 |
| Loan interest expense | 10,000 |
| Opening total equity (1 Jan 2026) | 250,000 |
| Cash dividends paid during 2026 (no new shares issued) | 30,000 |

**Inventory batches (FIFO cost flow — 800 units sold during 2026):**

| Date | Description | Units | Unit Cost | Total |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 Jan 2026 | Opening inventory | 200 | 40 | 8,000 |
| 14 Apr 2026 | Purchase | 500 | 44 | 22,000 |
| 9 Oct 2026 | Purchase | 400 | 50 | 20,000 |
| **Total available** | | **1,100** | | **50,000** |

**Non-current assets:** Workshop equipment was acquired for **120,000** with an estimated residual value of **20,000** and a useful life of **5 years** (straight-line depreciation).

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Under rising unit purchase prices, FIFO reports a higher closing inventory value and higher profit than AVCO.
   - **b.** Paying a cash dividend to shareholders is recorded as an operating expense in the income statement.
   - **c.** Prepaid rent at year-end is classified as a current asset on the Statement of Financial Position.
2. Using the **FIFO** method, calculate: (i) Closing inventory at 31 Dec 2026 *(5 points)*, (ii) Cost of sales (COGS) for 2026 *(5 points)*, and (iii) Gross profit *(5 points)*. *(15 points in total)*
3. Calculate the adjusted 2026 figures for: (i) Wages expense *(4 points)*, (ii) Rent expense *(4 points)*, (iii) Annual straight-line depreciation *(3 points)*, (iv) Operating profit (EBIT) *(4 points)*, and (v) Net profit for the year *(3 points)*. *(18 points in total)*
4. Calculate Closing Total Equity on the Statement of Financial Position at 31 Dec 2026. *(6 points)*

1b. Cash dividends are an income statement expense
1c. Prepaid rent is a current asset on the SFP

2026 Wages Expense (incl. year-end accrual)

wiseflowFields.group: 4. Statement of Financial Position Equity (6 pts)
wiseflowFields.label: Closing Total Equity at 31 Dec 2026

hints: Under FIFO, the 800 sold units use all 200 opening units (@£40), all 500 April units (@£44), and 100 October units (@£50), leaving 300 October units in closing inventory.

Add accrued wages (+£6,000), deduct prepaid rent (−£8,000), deduct straight-line depreciation ((120,000 − 20,000)/5 = £20,000) and bad debts (£4,000). Dividends reduce Retained Earnings directly, not Net Profit.
rubricChecks: Computed FIFO closing inventory (£15,000) and COGS (£35,000)
Adjusted wages (£146,000) and rent (£40,000) accurately under accruals
Kept dividends (£30,000) out of Net Profit (£110,000) and rolled forward Equity (£330,000)
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFA-E1 (45 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(dividends are an appropriation of retained earnings, not an expense)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **FIFO Inventory & Gross Profit:**
   - Available goods $= 8,000 + 22,000 + 20,000 = £50,000$ ($1,100$ units). Closing units $= 1,100 - 800 = 300$ units from 9 Oct batch $@ £50 = \mathbf{£15,000}$.
   - $\text{COGS} = 50,000 - 15,000 = \mathbf{£35,000}$ *(check: $200(40) + 500(44) + 100(50) = 8,000 + 22,000 + 5,000 = 35,000$)*.
   - $\text{Gross Profit} = 420,000 - 35,000 = \mathbf{£385,000}$.
3. **Operating & Net Profit:**
   - Wages expense $= 140,000 + 6,000 = \mathbf{£146,000}$ · Rent expense $= 48,000 - 8,000 = \mathbf{£40,000}$ · Depreciation $= (120,000 - 20,000)/5 = \mathbf{£20,000}$.
   - Total operating expenses $= 146,000 + 40,000 + 20,000 + 4,000 + 55,000 = £265,000 \implies \text{Operating Profit} = 385,000 - 265,000 = \mathbf{£120,000}$.
   - $\text{Net Profit} = 120,000 - 10,000 = \mathbf{£110,000}$.
4. **Closing Equity:** $250,000 + 110,000 - 30,000 = \mathbf{£330,000}$.
questions.pitfall: Subtracting dividends inside Net Profit, or forgetting to subtract residual value (£20,000) in straight-line depreciation.

pacing.rationale: 45-point WISEflow FLOWmulti exercise (45m exam par at 1 pt = 1 min; ±2% rounding margin).

questions.title: WFA-E2 · Bergen Marine Ltd · Indirect Statement of Cash Flows (35 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
The following summary financial information has been extracted for **Bergen Marine Ltd** for the financial year ended **31 December 2026** (all figures in **£m**; use a minus sign `-` for net outflows and negative balances):

| Statement / Balance Item | 1 Jan 2026 | 31 Dec 2026 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Property, plant & equipment (carrying amount / NBV) | 210 | 236 |
| Inventories | 30 | 39 |
| Trade receivables | 45 | 41 |
| Trade payables | 28 | 22 |
| Tax payable | 14 | 11 |
| Cash / (bank overdraft) | −10 | ? |

**Additional information for 2026 (£m):**

- **a)** Operating profit (EBIT) was **84**, stated after charging depreciation of **26** and a **loss on disposal** of equipment of **5**.
- **b)** The disposed equipment had a carrying amount (NBV) of **18** and was sold for **13** cash. All PPE additions were paid in cash.
- **c)** Interest paid in cash was **8**. Income statement tax charge was **16**.
- **d)** A new long-term bank loan of **20** was raised, and cash dividends of **12** were paid (classified under **Financing activities**).

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** A non-cash loss on disposal of non-current assets is added back to operating profit when reconciling to cash generated from operations, while the actual sale proceeds appear under investing activities.
   - **b.** Making a bonus issue of shares (capitalising reserves) generates a financing cash inflow.
   - **c.** Profitable rapidly growing firms can experience negative operating cash flows (overtrading) if working capital expands faster than cash profits.
2. Calculate: (i) Cash generated from operations before interest & tax *(5 points)*, (ii) Cash tax paid during 2026 *(4 points)*, and (iii) Net cash from operating activities *(4 points)*. *(13 points in total)*
3. Calculate: (i) Cash paid for PPE additions *(4 points)*, (ii) Net cash from investing activities *(4 points)*, and (iii) Net cash from financing activities *(4 points)*. *(12 points in total)*
4. Calculate the closing cash balance at 31 December 2026. *(4 points)*

wiseflowFields.label: 1a. Disposal loss add-back & investing proceeds
1b. Bonus share issue creates financing cash inflow
1c. Profitable growth can cause negative operating cash flow (overtrading)
Cash Generated from Operations (before interest & tax)
Cash Tax Paid during 2026 (enter positive magnitude 19 or -19)
Net Cash from Operating Activities (after interest 8 & tax paid)
Cash Paid for PPE Additions (magnitude 70 or -70)
Net Cash from Investing Activities (use minus sign)
Net Cash from Financing Activities
Closing Cash Balance at 31 Dec 2026

hints: Cash generated = Operating profit (84) + Depreciation (26) + Disposal loss (5) − ΔInventory (9) + ΔReceivables decrease (4) − ΔPayables decrease (6).
Roll forward PPE NBV: Opening (210) + Additions − Disposal NBV (18) − Depreciation (26) = Closing (236) ⇒ Additions = 70. Net investing = −70 + 13 disposal cash = −57.
rubricChecks: Added back both depreciation (26) and loss on disposal (5) in Operating cash
Reconciled Tax Paid (14 + 16 − 11 = 19) and PPE Additions (70) via roll-forward
Combined Opening Overdraft (−10) + Net Change (+28) = +18 Closing Cash
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFA-E2 (35 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(a bonus issue transfers reserves to share capital with zero cash flow)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Operating Activities (£m):**
   - $\text{Cash generated} = 84 + 26 + 5 - (39 - 30) + (45 - 41) - (28 - 22) = 115 - 9 + 4 - 6 = \mathbf{104}$.
   - $\text{Tax paid} = 14 + 16 - 11 = \mathbf{19}$.
   - $\text{Net cash from operating activities} = 104 - 8 - 19 = \mathbf{77}$.
3. **Investing & Financing Activities (£m):**
   - $\text{PPE Additions} = 236 - 210 + 18 + 26 = \mathbf{70} \implies \text{Net investing cash flow} = -70 + 13 = \mathbf{-57}$.
   - $\text{Net financing cash flow} = +20\text{ (loan)} - 12\text{ (dividends)} = \mathbf{+8}$.
4. **Closing Cash:** Net change $= 77 - 57 + 8 = +28 \implies -10 + 28 = \mathbf{+18\text{ (£m)}}$.
questions.pitfall: Subtracting disposal loss instead of adding it back, or forgetting disposal NBV (18) and depreciation (26) when solving for PPE additions.

questions.title: WFA-E3 · Oslo Mobility · Break-Even, Margin of Safety & Scarce Machine Hours (30 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Oslo Mobility Ltd** manufactures electric bicycles. Budgeted data for its existing **Commuter** model and a proposed **Cargo** model are shown below (all currency figures in GBP):

| Metric | Commuter | Cargo (Part B) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Selling price per unit | 500 | 750 |
| Variable cost per unit | 300 | 450 |
| Budgeted monthly sales (Part A) | 800 units | — |
| Maximum monthly market demand (Part B) | 600 units | 300 units |
| Specialised CNC machine time per unit | 2.5 MH | 5.0 MH |

Total monthly fixed costs are **120,000** in both Part A and Part B. In **Part B**, specialised CNC machine capacity is limited to **2,100 machine hours (MH)** per month.

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Margin of safety (%) measures the percentage by which budgeted sales can fall before the business incurs an operating loss.
   - **b.** When machine hours are the single scarce limiting factor, products should be ranked by highest contribution per unit of output.
   - **c.** An increase in the income tax rate raises the pre-tax sales volume required to earn a specified **after-tax** target profit.
2. **Part A (Single-product Commuter):** Calculate: (i) Break-even sales volume in units *(4 points)*, (ii) Margin of safety as a % of budgeted sales *(4 points)*, and (iii) Monthly units required to earn an operating profit of 70,000 *(4 points)*. *(12 points in total)*
3. **Part B (Scarce CNC capacity of 2,100 MH):** Calculate: (i) Commuter contribution per machine hour *(4 points)*, (ii) Optimal monthly units of Cargo to produce *(4 points)*, and (iii) Maximum monthly operating profit under the optimal mix *(4 points)*. *(12 points in total)*

hints: Unit CM for Commuter = £500 − £300 = £200. Margin of safety % = (Budgeted − BEP) / Budgeted × 100.
Rank by CM per scarce machine hour: Commuter = £200 / 2.5 MH = £80/MH vs Cargo = £300 / 5.0 MH = £60/MH. Fulfil Commuter's 600-unit demand first!
rubricChecks: Calculated BEP (600 units), MOS (25%), and target-profit volume (950 units)

questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Worked Solution · WFA-E3 (30 pts):**
1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Wrong** *(rank by contribution **per unit of the scarce resource**, £/MH)* · **1c. Right**.
2. **Part A (CVP):**
   - $\text{BEP} = 120,000 / (500 - 300) = \mathbf{600\text{ units}}$.
   - $\text{Margin of Safety \%} = (800 - 600)/800 \times 100 = \mathbf{25\%}$.
   - $\text{Target units} = (120,000 + 70,000)/200 = \mathbf{950\text{ units}}$.
3. **Part B (Scarce Machine Hours):**
   - Commuter: $£200 / 2.5\text{ MH} = \mathbf{£80/\text{MH}}$ (Rank 1) · Cargo: $£300 / 5.0\text{ MH} = £60/\text{MH}$ (Rank 2).
   - Produce max **600 Commuter** units ($600 \times 2.5 = 1,500\text{ MH}$). Remaining capacity $= 2,100 - 1,500 = 600\text{ MH} \implies 600 / 5.0 = \mathbf{120\text{ Cargo units}}$.
   - $\text{Max Operating Profit} = 600(200) + 120(300) - 120,000 = 120,000 + 36,000 - 120,000 = \mathbf{£36,000}$.
questions.pitfall: Dividing Margin of Safety by BEP (600) instead of budgeted sales (800), or prioritising Cargo because £300 > £200 per unit.

questions.title: WFA-E4 · Fjord Tech · NPV, Working Capital Recovery, Payback & ARR (30 pts)
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Fjord Tech AS** is evaluating a 4-year capital investment project with a cost of capital of **r = 10%**. Projected cash flows and asset data are summarized below (all currency figures in GBP):

| Period | Item | Amount |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| t = 0 | Equipment purchase outlay | −160,000 |
| t = 0 | Immediate working capital outlay (fully recovered at t = 4) | −20,000 |
| t = 1 | Net operating cash inflow (before depreciation) | 55,000 |
| t = 2 | Net operating cash inflow (before depreciation) | 65,000 |
| t = 3 | Net operating cash inflow (before depreciation) | 60,000 |

questions.title: WFB-M10 · Real vs nominal cash flows and discount rates
questions.promptMarkdown: When evaluating capital projects in the presence of general inflation, the golden consistency rule requires:
options: Discounting nominal (money) cash flows at the real cost of capital
Discounting real cash flows at the nominal (money) cost of capital

Ignoring inflation completely because sales prices and costs never change

**Solberg Energy AS** is choosing between two **mutually exclusive** 3-year projects at a cost of capital of **r = 12%** (no capital rationing; all currency figures in GBP):

1. **Right or Wrong:** **1a. Right** · **1b. Right** · **1c. Wrong** *(maximise NPV, not payback speed)*.
2. **Payback & NPV (12%):**

questions.title: WFD-M1 · Enhancing qualitative characteristics
questions.promptMarkdown: Which pair lists two **enhancing** (rather than fundamental) qualitative characteristics of useful financial information?
hints: Eliminate options that violate core accounting conventions or cash-flow vs accrual definitions.
questions.solutionMarkdown: **Correct: B.** The two *fundamental* qualities are relevance and faithful representation; the four *enhancing* qualities are comparability, verifiability, timeliness, and understandability.
questions.pitfall: Read underlined/bold qualifiers carefully — BI MCQs often flip one word such as 'profit' vs 'cash flow' or 'relevant' vs 'irrelevant'.

questions.title: WFD-M2 · Users of financial vs management accounting
questions.promptMarkdown: Which statement best distinguishes **management accounting** from financial accounting?
options: Management accounting must strictly follow IFRS reporting formats
Management accounting focuses exclusively on audited historical transactions
Management accounting is tailored to internal decision-makers and often uses forward-looking estimates
Management accounting is legally mandated for all limited companies once a year
hints: Eliminate options that violate core accounting conventions or cash-flow vs accrual definitions.
questions.solutionMarkdown: **Correct: C.** Management accounting serves internal managers, is not bound by IFRS, and frequently uses budgets, forecasts, and relevant future costs.
questions.pitfall: Read underlined/bold qualifiers carefully — BI MCQs often flip one word such as 'profit' vs 'cash flow' or 'relevant' vs 'irrelevant'.

questions.title: WFD-M3 · Expanded accounting equation
questions.promptMarkdown: Which equation correctly expresses the relationship among Assets (A), Liabilities (L), Opening Equity (E₀), Revenues (R), Expenses (Ex), and Owner Drawings (D)?
hints: Eliminate options that violate core accounting conventions or cash-flow vs accrual definitions.
questions.solutionMarkdown: **Correct: A.** Closing Equity equals `E₀ + Profit − Drawings = E₀ + (R − Ex) − D`, so `A = L + E₀ + (R − Ex) − D`.
questions.pitfall: Read underlined/bold qualifiers carefully — BI MCQs often flip one word such as 'profit' vs 'cash flow' or 'relevant' vs 'irrelevant'.

questions.title: WFD-M4 · Equity roll-forward profit calculation
questions.promptMarkdown: At the start of the year, a business had equity of `62,000`, and by year-end equity had risen to `74,500`. During the year, the owner withdrew `15,000` in cash for personal use and contributed equipment valued at `9,500`. What was the **profit or loss** for the year?
hints: Eliminate options that violate core accounting conventions or cash-flow vs accrual definitions.
questions.solutionMarkdown: **Correct: B (`18,000`).** `Closing Equity = Opening Equity + Capital Introduced + Profit − Drawings` ⇒ `74,500 = 62,000 + 9,500 + Profit − 15,000` ⇒ `Profit = 74,500 − 56,500 = 18,000`.
questions.pitfall: Read underlined/bold qualifiers carefully — BI MCQs often flip one word such as 'profit' vs 'cash flow' or 'relevant' vs 'irrelevant'.

questions.title: WFD-M5 · FIFO vs LIFO during deflation
questions.promptMarkdown: During a period of **falling** purchase prices (deflation), using the **FIFO** inventory valuation method instead of LIFO will report ______ at year-end.
options: higher profit and higher closing inventory
higher profit and lower closing inventory
lower profit and lower closing inventory
lower profit and higher closing inventory
hints: Eliminate options that violate core accounting conventions or cash-flow vs accrual definitions.
questions.solutionMarkdown: **Correct: C.** Under falling prices, FIFO charges older (more expensive) units to cost of sales (lower profit) and leaves newer (cheaper) units in closing inventory (lower inventory value).
questions.pitfall: Read underlined/bold qualifiers carefully — BI MCQs often flip one word such as 'profit' vs 'cash flow' or 'relevant' vs 'irrelevant'.

questions.title: WFD-M6 · Cost behaviour statements
questions.promptMarkdown:
Consider two statements concerning costs:
- **a)** Variable costs per unit remain constant within the relevant range of output.
- **b)** Sunk costs should be included in short-term special-order pricing decisions.

Which combination is correct?
hints: Eliminate options that violate core accounting conventions or cash-flow vs accrual definitions.
questions.solutionMarkdown: **Correct: B.** Variable cost per unit is constant within the relevant range (a is True); sunk/past costs are never relevant to future decisions (b is False).

questions.title: WFD-M7 · Opportunity cost relevance
questions.promptMarkdown: The contribution forgone by diverting a scarce resource from its next-best alternative use is known as a(n) ______ cost and is always **relevant**.
hints: Eliminate options that violate core accounting conventions or cash-flow vs accrual definitions.
questions.solutionMarkdown: **Correct: C.** An opportunity cost measures the cash/contribution sacrificed from the best foregone alternative and is always relevant to decision-making.
questions.pitfall: Read underlined/bold qualifiers carefully — BI MCQs often flip one word such as 'profit' vs 'cash flow' or 'relevant' vs 'irrelevant'.

questions.title: WFD-M8 · Full costing vs marginal costing
questions.promptMarkdown: Under **full (absorption) costing**, indirect manufacturing overheads are assigned to individual jobs primarily by:
options: expensing all overheads as period costs in the month incurred
applying a predetermined overhead recovery rate based on an activity driver such as labour or machine hours
dividing total revenue equally across every customer invoice
hints: Eliminate options that violate core accounting conventions or cash-flow vs accrual definitions.
questions.solutionMarkdown: **Correct: C.** Full costing absorbs production overheads into job/unit costs using a predetermined recovery rate (e.g. budgeted overhead ÷ budgeted DLH or MH).
questions.pitfall: Read underlined/bold qualifiers carefully — BI MCQs often flip one word such as 'profit' vs 'cash flow' or 'relevant' vs 'irrelevant'.

questions.title: WFD-M9 · Effect of higher cost of capital on NPV and IRR
questions.promptMarkdown: A conventional investment project has an initial cash outlay at t = 0 followed by positive net cash inflows in years 1–4. If the firm's **cost of capital increases**, what happens to the project's **NPV** and **IRR**?
options: NPV: Decrease and IRR: No change
NPV: Increase and IRR: No change
hints: Eliminate options that violate core accounting conventions or cash-flow vs accrual definitions.
questions.solutionMarkdown: **Correct: A.** Higher discount rates reduce the present value of future cash inflows (NPV decreases), whereas IRR depends solely on the project's cash flows and is unchanged.

questions.title: WFD-M10 · Relevant cost of existing machinery in NPV
questions.promptMarkdown: Nordvik AS owns a specialised press bought 3 years ago for `450,000` (current carrying value `270,000`). If not used on Project X, the press could be sold today for `140,000` or deployed on Project Y where it would save purchasing a replacement press for `195,000`. questions.title: Exercise 1: Measuring and reporting financial position
questions.promptMarkdown:
Nora started a new design business on **01. May**. To do so, she opened a business bank account and transferred **60,000** of her own money into it. During the first month of operations, the following additional transactions took place:

- **a)** She borrowed **40,000** from Oslo Commercial Bank and paid the money into the business bank account.
- **b)** She paid **48,000** cash for a small studio unit (premises).
- **c)** She paid **5,000** cash for a second-hand delivery van.
- **d)** She bought goods for resale (inventories) for **12,000**, paying immediately, and bought further goods for **24,000** on credit.
- **e)** She sold goods which had cost **18,000** for **32,000**. Of this revenue, **8,000** was received in cash and the remaining **24,000** was on credit.
- **f)** She paid **300** cash for fuel for the van, all of which was used during May.
- **g)** She received **9,000** cash from trade receivables.
- **h)** She paid **400** cash to Oslo Commercial Bank as interest on the loan for May.

Ignore depreciation of non-current assets.

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** The Statement of Financial Position sets out the assets of a business and the claims (equity and liabilities) against those assets at a specific point in time.
   - **b.** Inventories held for resale are classified as non-current assets because they are physical goods.
   - **c.** Under the dual aspect convention, every transaction affects at least two items so the accounting equation always remains in balance.
2. Open a beginning-of-May Statement of Financial Position for Nora's business (total assets and opening equity). *(6 points)*
3. Track transactions **a)** to **h)** as pluses and minuses to determine every end-of-May Statement of Financial Position balance (Cash, Trade receivables, Inventories, Trade payables, Borrowings). *(24 points)*
4. State the end-of-May **Total Assets** and **Closing Equity** on Nora's Statement of Financial Position. *(10 points)*
5. Calculate the **profit** Nora's business earned in May. *(4 points)*
hints: Start with Opening Cash = 60,000 and Opening Equity = 60,000, then adjust every cash inflow/outflow across a)–h).
Only transactions e) (+14,000 gross profit), f) (−300 fuel), and h) (−400 interest) affect profit.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**1. Right or wrong (6 pts):** `1a = Right`, `1b = Wrong` (inventories are current assets), `1c = Right`.

**2. Beginning-of-May SFP (6 pts):** Cash = `60,000` · Total Assets = `60,000` · Opening Equity = `60,000`.

**3. End-of-May balances (24 pts):**
- **Cash:** `60,000 + 40,000 − 48,000 − 5,000 − 12,000 + 8,000 − 300 + 9,000 − 400 = 51,300`
- **Trade receivables:** `24,000 − 9,000 = 15,000`
- **Inventories:** `12,000 + 24,000 − 18,000 = 18,000`
- **Trade payables:** `24,000` · **Borrowings:** `40,000`

**4. End-of-May SFP totals (10 pts):**
- Non-current assets: Premises `48,000` + Van `5,000` = `53,000`
- Current assets: Inventories `18,000` + Receivables `15,000` + Cash `51,300` = `84,300`
- **Total Assets:** `53,000 + 84,300 = 137,300`
- **Closing Equity:** `60,000 + 13,300 = 73,300` (`Equity 73,300 + Borrowings 40,000 + Payables 24,000 = 137,300 ✓`)

**5. May Profit (4 pts):** `(32,000 − 18,000) − 300 − 400 = 13,300` (transactions **e**, **f**, and **h** affect profit).
questions.pitfall: Receiving 9,000 from receivables (g) and borrowing 40,000 (a) change Cash, NOT profit!

questions.title: Exercise 2: Break-even analysis
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Lillehammer Services AS** provides a single standard service. The business's results for a representative month are as follows:

| Metric | Monthly Result |
| --- | ---: |
| Sales [units of service] | 800 |
| Sales revenue | 48,000 |
| Operating profit | 18,000 |

There were no changes in selling price or cost structure over the period. Variable costs were **15** per unit of service.

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Contribution per unit equals selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit.
   - **b.** Irrelevant costs include future differential cash flows.
   - **c.** At the break-even point, total contribution equals total fixed costs and operating profit is zero.
2. Calculate the **selling price per unit** and the **fixed costs per month**. *(6 points)*
3. Calculate the **break-even point** in units and in sales revenue. *(6 points)*
4. Calculate: (i) the **margin of safety (%)** at 800 units *(6 points)*, and (ii) the monthly **units required** to earn a target operating profit of **27,000** *(6 points)*. *(12 points in total)*
hints: Selling price = Sales revenue ÷ Units; Fixed costs = Total Contribution − Operating Profit.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**1. Right or wrong (6 pts):** `1a = Right`, `1b = Wrong` (future differential cash flows are relevant), `1c = Right`.

**2. Price & Fixed Costs (6 pts):**
- Selling price = `48,000 / 800 = 60` per unit
- Contribution per unit = `60 − 15 = 45`
- Total contribution = `800 × 45 = 36,000` ⇒ Fixed costs = `36,000 − 18,000 = 18,000`

**3. Break-even point (6 pts):**
- Break-even units = `18,000 / 45 = 400` units
- Break-even revenue = `400 × 60 = 24,000`

**4. Margin of Safety & Target Profit (12 pts):**
- Margin of safety (%) = `(800 − 400) / 800 × 100% = 50%`
- Target units for 27,000 profit = `(18,000 + 27,000) / 45 = 1,000` units
questions.pitfall: Never subtract total cost per unit instead of variable cost per unit when computing contribution!

1b. Irrelevant costs include future differential cash flows

questions.title: Exercise 3: Full costing
questions.promptMarkdown:
The following information has been taken from the budget for the forthcoming financial year of **Drammen Metalworks AS**:

| Budgeted Activity / Manufacturing Cost | Amount |
| --- | ---: |
| Direct labor hours [hours] | 80,000 |
| Machine hours [hours] | 60,000 |
| Direct labor | 480,000 |
| Indirect labor | 96,000 |
| Direct materials | 160,000 |
| Power | 32,000 |
| Factory heat and light | 8,000 |
| Machine maintenance | 40,000 |
| Cleaning material | 4,000 |
| Depreciation: factory | 100,000 |
| Depreciation: machinery | 280,000 |
| **Total manufacturing costs** | **1,200,000** |

All direct labor is paid at the same hourly rate.

For the specific order **"No 204"**, the following is required:
- Direct materials: **6,500**
- Direct labor hours: **3,000 [hours]**
- Machine hours: **1,400 [hours]**

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** Indirect costs are costs that cannot be directly measured in respect of a particular job or cost unit.
   - **b.** Direct labor and direct materials should be included in the overhead pool when calculating the overhead recovery rate.
   - **c.** Full cost information is used for inventory valuation and long-run pricing decisions.
2. Calculate the **overhead recovery rate** based on direct labor hours. *(4 points)*
3. Calculate the **direct labor cost**, **overheads absorbed**, and **full cost** for order **"No 204"** using the overhead rate based on direct labor hours. *(10 points)*
hints: Total overheads = Total manufacturing costs (1,200,000) minus Direct labor (480,000) and Direct materials (160,000).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**1. Right or wrong (6 pts):** `1a = Right`, `1b = Wrong` (direct costs are traced directly, never put into the overhead pool), `1c = Right`.

**2. Overhead recovery rate (4 pts):**
- Total indirect overheads = `1,200,000 − 480,000 − 160,000 = 560,000`
- Overhead recovery rate = `560,000 / 80,000 DLH = 7.00` per DLH

**3. Full cost for order "No 204" (10 pts):**

- Direct materials = `6,500`
- Direct labor = `3,000 × 6.00 = 18,000`
- Overheads absorbed = `3,000 × 7.00 = 21,000`
- **Full cost of order "No 204"** = `6,500 + 18,000 + 21,000 = 45,500`

questions.title: Exercise 4: Net present value
questions.promptMarkdown:
**Solheim Industri AS** considers implementing an investment project with a useful life of **three years**. To implement the project, Solheim needs to buy a machine in **t = 0** for **60,000**. At the end of the three years in **t = 3**, the machine can be sold for **12,000**.

The machine produces **1,200 units** of a product each year from **t = 1** until **t = 3** at variable cash costs of **12 per unit** (paid immediately). The sales pattern is as follows:

| Period | Price per Unit | Sales Quantity | Cash Collection Pattern |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| t = 1 | 34 | 1,200 | Immediate payment for 600 units; payment for 600 units in t = 2 |
| t = 2 | 30 | 1,200 | Immediate payment for 600 units; payment for 600 units in t = 3 |
| t = 3 | 30 | 1,200 | Immediate payment for all 1,200 units |

The cost of capital is **r = 0.1** (10%; discount factor for t = 3 is `0.7513`; the other discount factors need to be calculated).

### Requirements:

1. **Right or wrong?** *(6 points in total, 2 points each)*
   - **a.** The accounting rate of return (ARR) is the average accounting profit from the project expressed as a percentage of the average investment.
   - **b.** Payback period (PP) is the length of time until an initial investment generates cumulative operating profit equal to its cost.
   - **c.** Net present value (NPV) is the sum of the discounted values of all net cash flows from an investment.
2. Calculate the net cash flows for t = 1, t = 2, t = 3 and the **Net Present Value (NPV)** at 10%. *(14 points)*
3. Calculate the **net income** from the project for each period **t = 1**, **t = 2**, and **t = 3**. Assume straight-line depreciation of the machine. *(14 points)*
4. What is the **total present value (in t = 0)** of the periods' **residual income**? *(No extra calculation necessary.)* *(2 points)*
5. Is the **internal rate of return (IRR)** larger or smaller than **10%**? *(4 points)*
hints: Annual straight-line depreciation = (60,000 − 12,000) / 3 = 16,000; Preinreich–Lücke theorem guarantees PV(Residual Income) = NPV.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**1. Right or wrong (6 pts):** `1a = Right`, `1b = Wrong` (payback measures **cash flows**, not operating profit), `1c = Right`.

**2. Cash Flows & NPV at 10% (14 pts):**
- Variable cash outflow each year = `1,200 × 12 = 14,400`
- `CF₀ = −60,000`
- `CF₁ = (600 × 34) − 14,400 = 20,400 − 14,400 = 6,000`
- `CF₂ = (600 × 34) + (600 × 30) − 14,400 = 38,400 − 14,400 = 24,000`
- `CF₃ = (600 × 30) + (1,200 × 30) − 14,400 + 12,000 = 51,600`
- `NPV = −60,000 + 6,000/1.1 + 24,000/1.1² + 51,600/1.1³ = −60,000 + 5,454.55 + 19,834.71 + 38,767.84 = 4057.1`

**3. Accrual Net Income t = 1..3 (14 pts):**
- Straight-line depreciation = `(60,000 − 12,000) / 3 = 16,000` per year
- `NI₁ = (1,200 × 34) − 14,400 − 16,000 = 10,400`
- `NI₂ = (1,200 × 30) − 14,400 − 16,000 = 5,600`
- `NI₃ = (1,200 × 30) − 14,400 − 16,000 = 5,600`

**4. Total PV of Residual Income at t = 0 (2 pts):** By the Preinreich–Lücke theorem, `PV(RI) = NPV = 4057.1` (no extra calculation needed!).

**5. IRR vs 10% (4 pts):** Because `NPV > 0` at `10%` on a conventional investment, the IRR must be **Larger than 10%**.
questions.pitfall: Remember that Net Income uses invoiced accrual sales (1,200 units/yr) minus depreciation, whereas NPV uses cash collections and ignores depreciation!
